pos: n. (Olaus Petri, 1493–1552, preacher at Stockholm, the chief reformer of Sweden)
etymology: Latinised form of Swedish Olof Petersson: Olaus from Norse Anleifr, ancestral relic; Petri, son of Peter.
biblical_def: Olaus Petri was a smith's son of Örebro who studied at Wittenberg from 1516 to 1518 and heard Luther at the beginning; he came home a convinced evangelical and was made secretary to the city of Stockholm and then preacher at the Great Church there. From that pulpit he carried the Swedish Reformation almost single-handed. He preached in Swedish, married in 1525 while still in orders, debated the Roman party at Uppsala, and produced the books a new church needed: the Swedish New Testament of 1526, a handbook of the offices in 1529, a Swedish Mass in 1531, a postil, a catechism and a hymnbook. He also wrote a Swedish chronicle that made him suspect to the king. In 1539 he and Laurentius Andreae were tried for treason and condemned to death, the real offence being their resistance to Gustav Vasa's handling of church property; the sentences were commuted to fines. He died in 1552 as pastor of the church where he had begun. “For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a postil as a marginal note or a homily on the gospel, and counsel as advice, deliberation, or the purpose of God.
webster_full: POS'TIL, n. A marginal note; a short comment or exposition on a text of Scripture.
COUN'SEL, n. Advice; opinion or instruction given; design; purpose; the plan of God.
HAND'BOOK, n. A manual; a book of instruction to be held in the hand.
BOLD, a. Daring; courageous; intrepid; executed with spirit and freedom.
scriptures: For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God.
Jer 1:17
Thou therefore gird up thy loins, and arise, and speak unto them all that I command thee: be not dismayed at their faces, lest I confound thee before them.
And Micaiah said, As the LORD liveth, what the LORD saith unto me, that will I speak.
Pro 28:1
The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion.
corruption_summary: The Stockholm preacher who wrote Sweden a Testament, a Mass and a hymnbook.
corruption_paragraphs: The Swedish Reformation is habitually described as a royal operation in which the preachers were instruments of Gustav Vasa's need for money and his quarrel with Rome. Olaus Petri's own treason trial is the standing refutation. He was condemned to death by the king he is supposed to have served, for resisting the confiscation of what belonged to the churches, and the books he wrote were not commissioned by a chancery but produced out of a city pulpit.

The principle to recover is that a preacher's commission runs to the whole counsel of God, including the parts that embarrass his patron. Micaiah states the rule for a prophet standing before a king who wants a different answer: “As the LORD liveth, what the LORD saith unto me, that will I speak” (1Ki 22:14). Jeremiah is given the same charge with the same warning attached: “be not dismayed at their faces, lest I confound thee before them” (Jer 1:17).

pos: n. (Laurentius Petri, 1499–1573, first evangelical Archbishop of Uppsala, chief translator of the Swedish Bible)
etymology: Latinised form of Swedish Lars Petersson: Laurentius, of Laurentum, laurelled; Petri, son of Peter.
biblical_def: Laurentius Petri, younger brother of Olaus, studied at Wittenberg and was elected Archbishop of Uppsala in 1531, the first evangelical to hold the see and the man who gave the Church of Sweden its settled shape. He held the primacy for forty-two years and used them to build rather than to break: he presided over the translation committee that produced the complete Swedish Bible of 1541, the Gustav Vasa Bible, which did for Swedish what Luther's did for German; he resisted the king's attempts to reduce the church to a department of state; he fought off a German attempt to impose a Lutheran order foreign to Swedish usage; and in 1571 he obtained the Church Ordinance that governed Sweden for centuries. He kept the historic episcopate and the old church buildings while putting the Scriptures and the catechism at the centre, and the Swedish church has been marked by that combination ever since. He is the type of the builder who comes after the breaker. “that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an ordinance as a rule established by authority, and an archbishop as a chief bishop having jurisdiction over other bishops.
webster_full: OR'DINANCE, n. A rule established by authority; a permanent rule of action; an established rite.
ARCHBISH'OP, n. A chief bishop; a church dignitary of the first class.
PRI'MACY, n. The chief ecclesiastical station or dignity; the office of an archbishop.
SET in order, To adjust; to arrange; to reduce to method.
scriptures: Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee.
And they taught in Judah, and had the book of the law of the LORD with them, and went about throughout all the cities of Judah, and taught the people.
Mal 2:7
For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts.
corruption_summary: Forty-two years in the primacy, a Swedish Bible and a Church Ordinance.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is confessional impatience. Strict Reformed readers dismiss Laurentius for keeping bishops, vestments and much of the old ceremonial, and Roman writers cite the same retentions as proof that nothing really changed in Sweden. Both pass over the 1541 Bible and the catechism, which are what the Swedish people actually received.

The principle to recover is that reformation requires ordering as well as clearing, and that the ordering is the slower and less celebrated half of the work. Paul left Titus in Crete for exactly that: “that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5). Jehoshaphat's teaching circuit is the Old Testament pattern of what an archbishop with a new vernacular Bible should do with it: “And they taught in Judah, and had the book of the law of the LORD with them” (2Ch 17:9).

pos: n. (Laurentius Andreae, c. 1470–1552, archdeacon and chancellor of Sweden, architect of the breach with Rome)
etymology: Latinised form of Swedish Lars Andersson: Laurentius, laurelled; Andreae, son of Andrew.
biblical_def: Laurentius Andreae was archdeacon of Strängnäs and the most capable administrator in Sweden when Gustav Vasa made him chancellor of the realm in 1523. He had come to evangelical convictions through Olaus Petri, and he supplied what the preachers could not: the legal and political argument by which a kingdom left the Roman obedience. It was his contention that the goods of the church belonged to the community of believers and therefore might be applied by the realm to the realm's need, which carried the Diet of Västerås in 1527 and transferred the Swedish church to the crown. He lived to see the argument turned past what he had meant by it. When the king's exactions went beyond anything the preachers would defend, Andreae resisted and lost everything; in 1539 he was tried for treason with Olaus Petri and condemned to death, then spared, and he died in obscurity. He is the dictionary's warning about a churchman who lends the state a principle. “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help” (Psa 146:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chancellor as a high officer of state or of a church court, and a diet as an assembly of princes or estates.
webster_full: CHAN'CELLOR, n. A high judicial officer; in some countries, the first minister of state.
DI'ET, n. An assembly of princes or delegates for legislative or other purposes.
AR'CHDEACON, n. An ecclesiastical dignitary next in rank below a bishop.
IN'STRUMENT, n. One who or that which is subservient to the execution of a plan or purpose.
scriptures: Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help.
Pro 21:1
The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will.
Dan 2:21
And he changeth the times and the seasons: he removeth kings, and setteth up kings: he giveth wisdom unto the wise, and knowledge to them that know understanding:

Shall the axe boast itself against him that heweth therewith? or shall the saw magnify itself against him that shaketh it? as if the rod should shake itself against them that lift it up, or as if the staff should lift up itself, as if it were no wood.
corruption_summary: The chancellor whose argument carried Västerås and then consumed him.
corruption_paragraphs: Andreae is cited on both sides of a modern debate about church and state: by Erastians as the man who rightly subordinated ecclesiastical property to the common good, and by their opponents as the cautionary instance of a cleric who sold the church to a king. Neither reading attends to what actually happened, which is that he framed a true principle — that church goods are held in trust for the people of God — and watched a prince convert it into a title to the whole.

The principle to recover is that providence governs the rise and fall of statesmen and that the ablest instrument is still an instrument: “And he changeth the times and the seasons: he removeth kings, and setteth up kings” (Dan 2:21). Isaiah puts the question to any man who mistakes his usefulness for his standing: “Shall the axe boast itself against him that heweth therewith?” (Isa 10:15).

pos: n. (Hans Tausen, 1494–1561, called the Danish Luther, reformer of Denmark and bishop of Ribe)
etymology: Danish Hans, a contraction of Johannes, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Tausen, son of Tue.
biblical_def: Hans Tausen was a Johannite monk of Antvorskov who was sent abroad to study and used the liberty to go to Wittenberg in 1523, against his order's express direction. Brought home and confined at Viborg in Jutland, he preached through the window of his cell to the crowd outside, and the town carried him; by 1526 he was preaching openly, King Frederick I had taken him as a royal chaplain to shield him, and Viborg had become the capital of the Danish Reformation. He translated the Pentateuch and parts of the New Testament into Danish, wrote a hymnbook and a postil, and in 1530 drew up the Confession of Copenhagen, the forty-three articles that the evangelical preachers laid before the Diet. Under Christian III he was made bishop of Ribe and spent his last twenty years ordering that diocese. The window at Viborg is the picture worth keeping: a man under sentence, preaching to a street that could not be shut out. “Be not afraid, but speak, and hold not thy peace” (Act 18:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines plainness as openness, want of ostentation, and a confession as a formulary of the articles of faith.
webster_full: PLAIN'NESS, n. Openness; rough sincerity; artlessness; freedom from ambiguity.
CONFES'SION, n. A formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised; a creed.
CHAP'LAIN, n. An ecclesiastic who has a chapel, or who performs service in a family or to a prince.
MON'ASTERY, n. A house of religious retirement; a convent of monks.
scriptures: Act 18:9
Then spake the Lord to Paul in the night by a vision, Be not afraid, but speak, and hold not thy peace:
For our gospel came not unto you in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Ghost, and in much assurance; as ye know what manner of men we were among you for your sake.
Seeing then that we have such hope, we use great plainness of speech:
Heb 13:7
Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation.
corruption_summary: The monk who preached through his cell window and reformed Denmark.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the Danish Reformation's standard telling, in which the whole thing is a dynastic settlement imposed by Christian III in 1536 and the preachers are decorations on a royal decree. Tausen was preaching under confinement ten years before the decree, and the Confession of Copenhagen was the preachers' document, not the crown's.

The principle to recover is that the gospel comes with a manner as well as a message, and that the manner is plainness: “Seeing then that we have such hope, we use great plainness of speech” (2Co 3:12). Paul tells the Thessalonians that the power was not in the words alone — “For our gospel came not unto you in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Ghost, and in much assurance” (1Th 1:5) — which is the only account that explains a crowd standing in a Jutland street to hear a prisoner.

pos: n. (Peder Palladius, 1503–1560, first evangelical bishop of Zealand and superintendent of the Danish church)
etymology: Danish Peder, from Greek petros, a stone; Palladius, a latinised surname taken from Pallas, the goddess of wisdom.
biblical_def: Peder Palladius took his doctorate at Wittenberg under Luther and Melanchthon and was called home in 1537 to be bishop of Zealand, the first see of Denmark, ordained with the other new superintendents by Johannes Bugenhagen at Christian III's coronation. For twenty-three years he was in effect the working head of the Danish church. He visited every one of the three hundred and ninety parishes of his diocese in person, and the book he made out of those visitations — his Visitatsbog, written in plain Danish and addressed to congregations as he had actually spoken to them — is the most vivid record anywhere of what the Reformation looked like in a village. He helped translate the Danish Bible of 1550, wrote catechetical and liturgical books, and trained the first generation of evangelical clergy. His greatness was not in controversy but in the visitation: a bishop who went and looked. “Let us go again and visit our brethren in every city where we have preached the word of the Lord, and see how they do” (Act 15:36).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a visitation as the act of a superior who visits his clergy to inquire into their conduct, and a superintendent as one who has the oversight.
webster_full: VISITA'TION, n. The act of visiting; the object of a visit; the visit of a superior for inquiry into conduct.
SUPERINTEND'ENT, n. One who has the oversight and charge of something, with the power of direction.
OVERSEE'R, n. One who overlooks; a superintendent; a bishop.
PAR'ISH, n. The precinct or territorial jurisdiction of a secular priest, or the people under his care.
scriptures: And some days after Paul said unto Barnabas, Let us go again and visit our brethren in every city where we have preached the word of the Lord, and see how they do.
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
corruption_summary: The bishop who walked every parish in Zealand and wrote down what he found.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a managerial one much nearer our own day: oversight understood as the gathering of reports rather than the visiting of people. Palladius's Visitatsbog exists because he stood in the churches and talked to the congregations, and it records what no return could have told him — what the people believed, what they still did at the old shrines, and how the parson was living.

The principle to recover is that the oversight Scripture commits to elders is personal and local before it is anything else: “Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly” (1Pe 5:2). Paul's proposal to Barnabas is the plainest statement of the visitation principle in the New Testament, and it ends with a reason rather than a procedure: “and see how they do” (Act 15:36).

pos: n. (Gustav I Vasa, 1496–1560, king of Sweden, under whom the realm left the Roman obedience)
etymology: Swedish Gustav, from Norse elements meaning staff of the Goths; Vasa, a sheaf, from the family arms.
biblical_def: Gustav Vasa led the rising that expelled the Danes in 1521, was elected king in 1523, and held Sweden for thirty-seven years. He is the sovereign under whom the Swedish Reformation was carried, and the dictionary states his part without flattery. He protected Olaus Petri when the bishops wanted him silenced, allowed and funded the Swedish New Testament of 1526 and the whole Bible of 1541, and carried the Diet of Västerås in 1527, which put the church of the realm under the crown. He also stripped that church with a thoroughness that shocked the very preachers who had argued his case, took the bells and the plate, reduced the bishops to pensioners, and in 1539 had Olaus Petri and Laurentius Andreae condemned to death for resisting him. A king may be the means of a reformation without being a reformed man, and Scripture itself keeps the two questions apart. “All the ways of a man are clean in his own eyes; but the LORD weigheth the spirits” (Pro 16:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines confiscation as the act of condemning private property to public use, and a nursing father as a protector who cherishes.
webster_full: CONFISCA'TION, n. The act of condemning as forfeited, and adjudging to the public treasury.
NUR'SING FATHER, One who nourishes and protects, as a prince who fosters the church.
SOV'EREIGN, n. A supreme lord or ruler; one who possesses the highest authority without control.
MO'TIVE, n. That which incites to action; that which determines the choice of the will.

All the ways of a man are clean in his own eyes; but the LORD weigheth the spirits.

And kings shall be thy nursing fathers, and their queens thy nursing mothers: they shall bow down to thee with their face toward the earth, and lick up the dust of thy feet; and thou shalt know that I am the LORD: for they shall not be ashamed that wait for me.

And the king stood in his place, and made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD, and to keep his commandments, and his testimonies, and his statutes, with all his heart, and with all his soul, to perform the words of the covenant which are written in this book.
Jer 17:5
Thus saith the LORD; Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD.
corruption_summary: The king who gave Sweden a Bible and took the church's bells.
corruption_paragraphs: Gustav Vasa is the standing exhibit for the claim that the Reformation was politics in a cassock: a prince wanting the church's revenues found a doctrine that let him take them. The dictionary grants the fact and denies the inference. The confiscations were real and indefensible, and the preachers said so at the cost of a capital sentence; that is precisely why the doctrine cannot be reduced to the policy. A gospel invented to serve a king does not produce men who go to trial against him.

The principle to recover is that God uses magistrates without endorsing them, and that the promise of royal protection in Isaiah — “And kings shall be thy nursing fathers, and their queens thy nursing mothers” (Isa 49:23) — is a promise about God's provision and not a licence for the nursing father. Jeremiah supplies the balance the Swedish church learned the hard way: “Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm” (Jer 17:5).

pos: n. (Christian III, 1503–1559, king of Denmark and Norway, who established the Reformation there in 1536)
etymology: Christian, a follower of Christ, from Greek Christianos; a dynastic name of the house of Oldenburg.
biblical_def: Christian III heard Luther at the Diet of Worms in 1521 as a prince of eighteen and never afterwards doubted the cause. He won the civil war called the Count's Feud and entered Copenhagen in 1536, and in that year arrested the bishops, declared the episcopal order dissolved, and had the Diet transfer their lands to the crown and their office to evangelical superintendents. He then sent for Johannes Bugenhagen of Wittenberg, who crowned him, ordained the seven new superintendents, and drafted with the Danish theologians the Church Ordinance of 1537 that governed Denmark and Norway for generations. Christian also paid for the Danish Bible of 1550 that bears his name and made it compulsory in every parish church. His Reformation was a settlement imposed from above on a kingdom that had been preparing for it from below for fifteen years, and it held. “he did it with all his heart, and prospered” (2Ch 31:21) is the chronicler's formula for a reforming king; the record of 1536 is less clean than that.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an ordinance as an established rite or rule, and to establish as to settle or fix firmly, to enact permanently.
webster_full: ESTAB'LISH, v. To settle or fix firmly; to enact or decree by authority for permanence.
OR'DINANCE, n. A rule established by authority; an established rite or ceremony.
SUPERINTEND'ENT, n. One who has the oversight and charge of something, with the power of direction.
RE'ALM, n. A kingdom; a king's dominions.

He in the first year of his reign, in the first month, opened the doors of the house of the LORD, and repaired them.
Neh 2:18

Then I told them of the hand of my God which was good upon me; as also the king's words that he had spoken unto me. And they said, Let us rise up and build. So they strengthened their hands for this good work.
Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
corruption_summary: The king who dissolved the Danish episcopate and paid for the Danish Bible.
corruption_paragraphs: The Danish Reformation is the favourite instance of the claim that northern Protestantism was simply the nationalisation of church property by solvent princes. The claim is not baseless and the dictionary will not pretend otherwise: bishops were arrested, estates were seized, and the crown ended the richer. What the account omits is Hans Tausen preaching at Viborg a decade earlier and the Confession of Copenhagen of 1530, which was the preachers' work and which the settlement of 1536 enacted rather than invented.

The principle to recover is that the magistrate's sword is a real and God-given office with a defined end — “For he is the minister of God to thee for good” (Rom 13:4) — and that a prince who uses it to establish true religion has done something a prince may do, which does not sanctify every seizure he makes along the way. Hezekiah's first act is the good example to hold up against the mixed one: “in the first year of his reign, in the first month, opened the doors of the house of the LORD” (2Ch 29:3).

pos: n. (Geble Pedersson, c. 1490–1557, first evangelical bishop of Bergen and the reformer of Norway)
etymology: Norwegian Geble, a form of Gabriel, man of God; Pedersson, son of Peder.
biblical_def: Geble Pedersson was a Norwegian who had studied abroad and come home with evangelical convictions, and in 1537 he was the one man in the country fit to be the first Protestant bishop of Bergen. Norway received the Reformation as a consequence of the Danish settlement rather than by any movement of its own: the last Roman archbishop fled to the Netherlands with the cathedral treasure, the monasteries were dissolved by decree, and a people who had asked for nothing were given a new church order in a Danish book. Geble's twenty years were spent making that decree into something real. He founded and endowed the Latin school at Bergen that trained the next generation, kept what men he could find and taught them himself, housed students in his own residence, and was remembered by his contemporaries chiefly for mildness in a situation where severity would have been easy and useless. “I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase” (1Co 3:6) is the whole account of such a ministry.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to endow as to furnish with a permanent fund, and increase as augmentation, growth, that which is added.

corruption_summary: Norway's first evangelical bishop, who built a school because he could not build a movement.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a historiographical embarrassment: because Norway's Reformation came by Danish decree, it is often written off as no reformation at all, and the men who had to work it out on the ground are passed over as agents of a foreign administration.

The principle to recover is that the kingdom of God advances by small and slow means which look like nothing while they are working: “For who hath despised the day of small things?” (Zec 4:10). The Lord's own figure for it is the one that fits a bishop endowing a grammar school in a town that did not ask for him: “The kingdom of heaven is like unto leaven, which a woman took, and hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened” (Mat 13:33).

pos: n. (Christiern Pedersen, c. 1480–1554, Danish humanist and translator, called the father of Danish literature)
etymology: Danish Christiern, a form of Christian; Pedersen, son of Peder.
biblical_def: Christiern Pedersen was a canon of Lund who went to Paris, learned the new printing and the new learning, and spent his life putting books into Danish. Before the Reformation reached him he had already printed the first Danish grammar aids, a Danish postil, and the Latin chronicle of Saxo; he then followed Christian II into exile, met the evangelical faith in the Netherlands and at Wittenberg, and turned his whole craft over to the Scriptures. He published the New Testament in Danish in 1529 and the Psalms in 1531, and when Christian III ordered a complete Danish Bible it was Pedersen's renderings, revised by the theologians, that carried most of it; the Bible of 1550 is substantially his Danish. He was a printer, a lexicographer, a grammarian and a translator rather than a preacher, and the Danish language as it was written for the next three centuries is largely his work. “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it” (Hab 2:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a lexicographer as the author of a dictionary, and to print as to take an impression of letters upon paper.
webster_full: LEXICOG'RAPHER, n. The author of a lexicon or dictionary.
PRINT, v. To take an impression of letters or figures upon paper; to publish by the press.
GRAM'MAR, n. The art of speaking or writing a language with propriety.
PLAIN, a. Evident to the understanding; clear; not obscure or difficult.

corruption_summary: The canon of Lund whose Danish became the Danish Bible.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern separation of the literary from the religious: Pedersen is honoured in Denmark as the father of the written language and his Bible work is treated as one project among several, when in fact the language took the shape it has because he was translating Scripture into it.

The principle to recover is that God commands his word to be written and written plainly, and that the labour of making a tongue capable of carrying it is part of the obedience. The charge to Habakkuk puts legibility in the command itself: “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it” (Hab 2:2). Luke's preface shows the same care in an evangelist — “to write unto thee in order” (Luk 1:3) — and order in a language is a grammarian's gift to the church.

pos: n. (Mikael Agricola, c. 1510–1557, bishop of Turku, translator of the Finnish New Testament and founder of written Finnish)
etymology: Finnish Mikael, from Hebrew Mikael, who is like God; Agricola, Latin for husbandman, a scholar's name taken for his father's calling.
biblical_def: Mikael Agricola was a Finnish peasant's son who studied at Wittenberg from 1536 to 1539 with a recommendation from Luther himself, came home as rector of the cathedral school at Turku, and in 1554 was made the first evangelical bishop of that see. He found a people whose language had never been printed. In 1543 he published the Abckiria, a primer and catechism that is the first book ever printed in Finnish; in 1544 a prayer book; in 1548 the Finnish New Testament, translated from the Greek with Erasmus and Luther at his elbow; and afterwards portions of the Old Testament and the liturgical books. He had to invent a written language to do it, and the orthography and much of the religious vocabulary of modern Finnish are his. He died at forty-seven on the road home from a peace embassy to Moscow. One man gave a nation its letters and its Testament in the same fourteen years. “because that every man heard them speak in his own language” (Act 2:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an abecedarian as one who teaches or is learning the alphabet, and orthography as the art of writing words with the proper letters.
webster_full: ABECEDA'RIAN, n. One who teaches the letters of the alphabet, or a learner of the letters.
ORTHOG'RAPHY, n. The art of writing words with the proper letters, according to common usage.
PRI'MER, n. A small elementary book for religious instruction, or for teaching children to read.
HUS'BANDMAN, n. A farmer; a cultivator or tiller of the ground.
scriptures: Act 2:6
Now when this was noised abroad, the multitude came together, and were confounded, because that every man heard them speak in his own language.
Therefore if I know not the meaning of the voice, I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian, and he that speaketh shall be a barbarian unto me.
Rev 14:6
And I saw another angel fly in the midst of heaven, having the everlasting gospel to preach unto them that dwell on the earth, and to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people,
Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
corruption_summary: The man who invented written Finnish in order to print a catechism in it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Agricola is claimed in Finland as a national founder and the religious purpose of the work is sometimes handled as the period costume of a linguistic achievement. He did not set out to create a literature; he set out to put a catechism and a Testament into the hands of Finns, and the literature is what that cost.

The principle to recover is that the gospel is for every tongue by express promise, and that a tongue with no letters must therefore be given letters: “having the everlasting gospel to preach unto them that dwell on the earth, and to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people” (Rev 14:6). Paul states the problem Agricola faced from the hearer's side: “Therefore if I know not the meaning of the voice, I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian” (1Co 14:11).
